opening_message:
Ticket 1: Douglas Salinas (employee ID E045) requests write access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E045.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Douglas Salinas (E045) is a full-time Engineer. Requested write access to Payroll. Full-time employees may have up to write; admin would require owning the system, which does not apply here. Recommend granting write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Engineer
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB shows Douglas Salinas (E045) is a contractor with basic security training. Contractors without advanced training may have at most read. Requested write exceeds the maximum, so grant read.
reason: Ticket 1: Douglas Salinas (E045) requested write access to Payroll. The two team notes conflict on employment type: one lists full_time (Engineer) allowing write, while the Security DB note lists contractor with basic security training. Per policy, contractors without advanced security training may have at most read. Given the conflicting facts, I apply the more restrictive, verified-by-Security status: contractor with basic training, so the maximum is read. Requested write exceeds the maximum; granting read.

- Note 2 says contractor with basic security training, recommends read.

According to the policy:
1. full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Engineer role doesn't own Payroll (Payroll owned by Payroll Specialist). So full-time Engineer max = write. Requested write => grant write.
2. contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. Basic training => max read. Requested write exceeds max => grant read.

Note 2: role Engineer, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation read. This reads like Security DB.
